link.title: Lecture notes: Towards and Algorithmic Theory of Machine Learning via Kernel Methods

entry.content:
These are personal lecture notes. They may be incomplete or contain mistakes; please consult the original course material for authoritative statements.

Main idea

The operator theoretic bridge between machine learning, algorithmic information theory, and dynamical systems are kernel methods.

Compression, learning and inference are manifestation of the same principle.

Principle of Occam from Solomonov Induction Algorithmic nature of simplicity - compute through kernel methods Eigenvalues of an integral operator, associated with a kernel. Kernel build from Kolmogorov complexity.

Short program - large weights larger eigenvalues - faster rates simple hypothesis - higher posterior

Why solomonoff induction is interesting to look at - the problem of induction.

Simplification of Dynamical systems is kind of compression, so reduction of Kolmogorov Complexity, from non-linear PDE to linear PDE or other methods.

Kernel complexity (KC) via MDL Kolmorogov KC as a measure of similarity. HSIC is approximating AMI somehow?

Complexity spectral correspondence via KC-spaces

Special kind of RKHS called Solomonoff Kernels and Solomonoff Gaussian Processes

Big takeaway is when the program length and complexity is manifesting itself in spectral mass.

Compression -> Spectrum -> Learning -> Learning Speed -> Compressibility

What is exactly the solomonoff prior, why is ideal, and why is not computable

Computable surrogate leads to the solomonoff kernel.

entry.title: Learning log: Dynamical Systems
entry.content:
Lecture 1

History of Dynamical Systems

High points, the beginning was in 1666, with Isaac Newton as 24 years old, invents ODEs.

Explains planetary orbits, 2 body problem, elliptical orbits because of gravity.

3 body problem is difficult (the problem of the moon), Gauss, Newton, Euler all fail.

Poincare explains that the 3 body problem cant be solved, using a geometric approach instead of calculus, and observes chaos for the first time.

The Geometric approach is called phase space. (People like to say Poincare discovered chaos)

Key ingredients of chaos: A phenomonenon occuring in deterministic systems, (no randomness, present state determines future states) We observe aperiodic seemingly unpredictable behaviour in deterministic systems. No equilibrium and doesnt settle down.

It displays sensitive dependence on initial conditions.

Errors get too big and move apart exponentially fast making predictability hard.

Late 1800 and 1900, physics is raging about Quantum mechanics while Poincares work goes unnoticed since its classical mechanics.

1920-1950- Nonlinear oscillators in physics. Engineering - radio, vacuum tube with a non-linear oscillator. radar, phase locked loops etc.

1950- computers invented 1960- Lorenz from MIT uses the computer - chaotic systems modelling convection in the atmosphere.

Deterministic aperiodic flow, also ignored, because journal for publishing was different from what Physicists and Mathematicians read.

Kolomogorov,Arnold and Moser (KAM) theory- following the stream of Poincare a pure math approach.

1975 - Bob May noticies chaos in iterated maps, simplified models of population.

Simple nonlinear systems with very complicated dynamics.

Logistic equation in population biology.

Mandelbrot starts fractals, which was ultimately related to chaos.

Winfree - biological rhythms, non-linear oscillators in biology.

Ruelle and Takens - chaos and turbelence, in the navier stokes equations and real fluid systems.

1978 - Feigenbaum, Logistic map and other iterated maps connects to phase transitions. Universal route to chaos - across different systems that had nothing in common at a scientific level. Statistical physics and phase transitions.

1980 - Chaos and nonlinear dynamics, fractals get traction. Featured in jurrasic park even.

1990 - Engineering applications of chaos etc.

Math of Dynamical Systems - the big picture

Logical structure of dynamics (Anything that changes in time)

Differential equations: $\dot{\boldsymbol{x}}=f(\boldsymbol{x})$ where $\boldsymbol{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $\boldsymbol{x}= { x_1, \dots, x_n } $

$\mathbb{R}^n$ is the phase space. and $\boldsymbol{x}$ is the state space.

In components

\[\begin{align*} \dot{x}_1 &= f_1(x_1,\dots,x_n) \\ &\vdots\\ \dot{x}_n &= f_n(x_1,\dots,x_n) \end{align*}\]

$f1, \dots, f_n$ given function, we say system is linear if all $x_i$ on RHS appear to the first power only.

Autonomous systems, where time doesnt appear in the RHS. To make it time dependent just consider $\dot{t}=1$, we only consider autonomous systems in this course to preserve the nice geometric properties.

Non-linear systems examples

Simple Harmonic oscillator: $m\ddot{x} + kx = 0$ To convert it into $\dot{\boldsymbol{x}}=f(\boldsymbol{x})$

We can easily rexpress it as $x_1=x$ and $x_2=dot{x}$

With this choice we can write $\dot{x_1}=x_1$ and $\dot{x_2}=\frac{-kx_1}{m}$

First power for $x_2$ and $x_1$ linear second order system.

Pendulum on the other hand $\ddot{x} + \sin{x}=0$ With $\dot{x_1}=x_2$ and $\dot{x_2}=-\sin{x_1}$, but the second term is non-linear 2nd order.

For small pertubations can be approximately linear, but for big movements most definitely non linear.

Elliptic functions, etc are taught but in the course we will use pictures.

Solution $(x_1(t), x_2(t)) \to$ point moving along a trajectory in space with coordinates $x_1,x_2$.

Think about trajectories in phase spaces.

Poincares big idea is, we can do the constructions in reverse. Construct what the trajectories look like.Therby gain information about the solution without solving it analytically.

Phase portrait

Phase portrait is a picture of all qualitatively different trajectories. We’ll without solving the differential equation analytically.

Types $n=1$ $n =2$ $n=3$ $n > 3$ $n=\infty (continuum)$
Linear RC circuit simple harmonic oscillator     maxwell equations, wave equation,schrodinger eqn
Non-linear Logistic growth pendulum     general relativity, turbulence, fibrilation in heart

PDEs, for linear in the continuum.

Phase Space and an examples: Chap 2

$\dot{x}= f(x), \quad x \in \mathbb{R}$.

1-D systems Examples $\dot{x} = \sin(x)$ single dimensional non linear

Standard approach is by change over variables But turns messy even for $\sin(x)$

The velocity interpretation, where particle moves on the x axis, then $\dot{x}$ is interpreted as velocity, and we can see the particle moves right when positive and left when negative. There are places where the velocity is zero, those are fixed points.

Stable and unstable fixed points.

entry.title: Learning log: Machine Learning Theory
entry.content:
I am currenty watching the youtube series on Machine Learning Theory, taught by Shai-Ben David from the University of Waterloo in 2015. I document my understanding of the lectures here. If you are reading this and spot some errors in my understanding / have tips for better exposition, or have a different model than mine, please reach out to me at email Would love to hear from you.

Why learning theory, whats the broad vision?

I am planning on starting graduate studies soon, and while the topic is still undecided I am inclined towards doing something in the interesection of control-theory and machine-learning. My inclination is to do some fundamental/deeply theoretic work. Therefore trying to get the basics right before starting to contribute to the theory myself.

Lecture 1

What is learning?

Learning is defined as the conversion of experience to expertise. To motivate learning we looked at some examples of learning in animals. Animals adapt their behaviours based on experiences they have.

Example 1: Rats exhibiting bait shyness. Rats will only consume a small bit of poisoned food, observe how they feel before eating more

Takeaway: The rat learns to observe, some relation between their consumption of the bait and them feeling nauseous and therefore modifies their behaviour to not consume the food.

Example 2: Pigeons and their spurious attributions. If you surround pigeons with some toys, they will peck on it, and simultaneously if you sprinkle food, completely unrelated to the toy they will make a misassociation between their pecking on the toy and the food.

Takeaway: It is possible to have superstitions or spurious correlations, and one must use common sense to rule out nonsensical explanations, we as humans are also perhaps susceptible to this, however we must figure out a way to bake in what reasonable relations are.

Example 3: Bait shyness, but with some modifications, we observe that if we replace the feeling of nausea for the rat with electrical shocks or the eating of the food with some other auditory signal, then there is no update in behaviour of the rats.

Takeaway: The behavioural adaptation of the rat strongly depends on some prior information on what may or may not affect the feeling of nausea as demonstrated by this experiment (this is probably baked into the rat from years of evolution), in the scenarios where such associations are not commonly observed its unlikely the rat changes its behaviour.

Why should we be interested in Machine Learning?

I think I dont really need to motivate myself to be interested in this topic, but still it makes sense to rehash whats the relevance of machine learning.

  • Not all rules are programmable or can be explained easily
  • Humans may not be able to solve some complex problems
  • Adaptivity - funnily enough, still in 2026 this continues to be a big problem, however back then the discussion was a fixed rule remains fixed, if programmed once, but a machine learner may conditioned on new data be able to adapt to new situations.

One thing to note is that machine learning may be inspired from learning in animals or nature. But we should not aim to mimic it, there may be better ways of learning and being more efficient and scalable.

Lecture 2

Big idea in this lecture was basically introducing inductive bias and defining ERM within the class of hypothesis.

A formal model for learning

We consider the following objects in our formal model We consider the domain set $\mathcal{X}$. We consider the label set $\mathcal{Y}$. The learner takes as input samples $S = \{(x_1,y_1),\dots, (x_2,y_2)\}$ The output of the learner is a rule $h(x)$ defined on any input $x$.

Running example for explaining the story, We shall consider the case of predicting the taste of papayas based on two attributes, softness and color. The labels for the papaya is tasty or not tasty, and therefore $\mathcal{Y} := {0,1}$

Given this formal model, we define a way to evaluate our output. To do so we introduce the first strong assumptions in our modelling. We assume that there exists a function $f: \mathcal{X} o \mathcal{Y}$, which determines the output of any input $x$.

Secondly we assume our inputs to the model are distributed according to $D$. We dont make any further assumptions on the form of $D$, and don’t assume we know this.

There is one more strong assumption that we make, that is the inputs are sampled iid from the distribution $D$.

Under these assumptions we can define

\(L_{D,f}(h)=\mathbb{P}_D[\{h(x) eq f(x)\}]\) our evaluation for a learners output $h$.

How to interpret this evaluation. Here we say that our learner performs badly, when the output of the learner disagrees with the true label. However, with a small caveat that we don’t care about all inputs equally, we only care about the inputs depending on how likely they are to appear in the population.

This evaluation cannot be done in practise, because this requires access to $D$ that we dont have. In literature this loss, may also be referred to as risk. And the objective of a learner is to output a training rule which minimises this risk.

However, as we explained above this is not possible in practise, because of our lack of knowledge of $D$. Instead we can define the empirical risk. The empirical risk is defined on the samples $S$.

So we shall define it as \(L_S(h) = rac{|\{i \in [m]: h(x_i) eq f(x_i)\}|}{m}\)

And our hope shall be if we minimize this empirical risk, we shall also perform well on the true risk.

And here we shall run into our first problem. Lets assume a decision rule for a set of samples $S$ which produces the correct labels for all samples $S$, but produces incorrect labels for all samples not in $S$.

So in our running example

Lecture 3

Big ideas were introduction to Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) Learning.

Relaxation of the realisability principle maybe, there is no function f generating the data instead there is just some distribution.

So the goal in this lecture was to basically bound the error with respect to this distribution.

Lecture 4

From classification to continous spaces etc

Generalised theory of learning some domain Z, set of models M and some loss function evaluation a model on a given instance.

Data generated by some unknown distribution, over Z

Our aim is to find the best model for this unknown distribution.

Loss is defined wrt distribution D of some model H as the expectation,

\[L_D(h) = \mathbb{E}_{Z\sim D} l(h,z)\]

So far Z is some distribution on $X imes {0,1}$ M is function from $X$ to $\{0,1\}$ \(l(h,\underbrace{(x,y)}_z) = egin{cases} 1 & h(x) eq y\ 0 & h(x)=y\ \end{cases}\)

Generalisation to multiclass prediction as an example. $l(h,(x,y))$ still is basically if you got the label right or wrong, however under the expectation it is generalisation.

In regression, the squared distance loss is pretty common to use as a loss $l(h,(x,t))$, where there is notion of a big or small mistake thats $(h(x)-t)^2$ square loss. We try to find a rule to minimise this loss. What we learn about statistical learning theory still valid here.

Clustering, representing data by some k code words. $Z \in \mathbb{R}^d$ where $M=$ vectors of k members of $\mathbb{R}^d$.

$h = {c_1, \dots, c_k}$ Every signal coded by one of the code words. We pay the cost of distortion.

Agnostic PAC Learning is very general, examples above illustrate the same.

#### First Learning Paradigm - Learning via Uniform Convergence

We dont know the distribution $D$, but know a sample. So how well does the sample represent the distribution.

Definition: A sample $S=(Z_1, \dots, Z_n)$ or $S=((x_1,y_1),\dots (x_n,y_n))$ is $\epsilon$ representative of class $H$ wrt a distribution $D$, if $ orall H$ $|L_S(h)-L_s(D)|\leq \epsilon$.

Where $L_s(h)= rac{1}{m}\sum_{z\in S}l(h,z)$

Good sample if loss measured on the sample is close to the true loss.

If we know the sample is a good representation how do we find a good hypothesis wrt the sample. Simply do ERM, wrt sample.

Claim : If S is $\epsilon$-representative of H wrt D, ERM_H functions h_s \(L_D(h_s) \leq \min_{h\in H}(L_D(h)) + 2\epsilon\)

What this means is if your sample is representative then optimising wrt samples gives you a pretty good guarantee that you are optimising wrt the distribution.

entry.title: Takeaways from RLSS 2026
entry.content:
I attended the Reinforcement Learning Summer School in Milan, this year. I had a fantastic time, and the lectures were very informative. While my long term goal remains, compiling all my learnings in the form of a lecture script, that is a non-trivial effort. In the meantime I have tried to write down the big ideas, as with enough effort I am sure, I am able to recall the proofs, and exact methods in the lectures. However, perhaps more useful for me (and the readers) might be the key takeaways.

MDPs and Dynamic Programming

The biggest learnings were the formal definitions of an Markov Decision Process. The fact that a Markov Decision Process is not just the environment, but rather the environment consisting of the transition kernel, and the policy.

Second the principle of Dynamic programming is breaking down a bigger problem into smaller components to solve them, it was named as such because back then it sounded cool and was a reason to get funding.

Evaluation of a policy, by introducing the value function $V$ and the $Q$ functions and by the Bellman expectation equations (which is just linear alegbra).

Proof for a unique policy was by Banach fixed point theorem, the Bellman operator $T^\pi$ is a sup-norm contraction. Intuition, from the proof we saw that $\gamma$ was hidden in the proof, and why bigger $\gamma$ implied slower convergence.

Optimizing a policy: This part provided the backbone of value based control. Essentially the thing to show here was the optimal Bellman contraction $T^\star$ also was a $\gamma$ contraction with respect to sup-norms. And consequently that the unique fixed point for $T^\star$ is $V^\star$ and $Q^\star$. The implication of this was if we solved fixed point equation $T^\star Q = Q$ then acting greedily is optimal policy.

Based on this we can make some algorithms, so we looked at the classic algorithms such as Value Iteration for evaluation a policy, again using Banach fixed point theorem to show convergence. An important insight was we need asynchronous value iteration for optimal control, with the convergence criterion being every state action pair is visited infinitely often. The big idea behind Q-learning.

We looked at policy iteration with the big insight being that we parameterise the policy and calculate the value function of that policy and with each step we greedily improve the policy and by monotinicity of the Bellman operator, we saw that if we act greedily with some policy $\pi$, thats $\pi’ = \textrm{greedy}(Q^\pi)$ then $\pi’$ is an improvement over $\pi$ and if it doesnt improve its converged.

RL 1

I am well aware that the title to this lecture is a bit uninformative, but the content wasn’t so perhaps bear with me.

In the last lecture, we assumed that the environment is known to us, the problem is with tractability of the planning procedure so to say.

However, if our model is not known to us, we must learn this from data and act according to the learn model. This comes under the purview of model-based RL. If we act according to an estimated model, the policy based on this model is bottlenecked by the estimation of the model.

entry.title: Sampling from Hard Distributions
entry.content:
I have found that sampling only becomes intuitive once it stops looking like a mysterious numerical trick. At its core, it is a way of replacing a calculation we cannot do with a calculation that we can: draw a lot of sensible random values, and let their average tell us something useful. That sounds almost too simple, but it gets us surprisingly far.

The interesting part is that this simple idea is enough to handle distributions for which even the normalising constant is out of reach. Let us get there gradually.

Probability and Inference

Before getting to sampling, I find it useful to remember where the distributions come from. The two probability rules I return to most often are the sum rule and the product rule. For two events $A$ and $B$,

\[P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\]

and

\[P(A \cap B) = P(A \mid B)P(B).\]

The product rule is especially useful because we can write it in either direction. Equating the two ways of writing the joint probability gives Bayes’ rule:

\[p(\theta \mid D) = \frac{p(D \mid \theta)p(\theta)}{p(D)}, \qquad p(D) = \int p(D \mid \theta)p(\theta)\,d\theta.\]

Here $D$ is the data and $\theta$ is whatever the model is trying to learn. If we only want one best answer, maximum likelihood chooses one value,

\[\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{ML}} = \arg\max_{\theta} p(D \mid \theta),\]

which is often a perfectly reasonable thing to do. The Bayesian view instead keeps the whole posterior $p(\theta \mid D)$. I like thinking of it as refusing to throw uncertainty away too early: we can say not only what seems most plausible, but also how unsure we are about it.

The slightly annoying term is $p(D)$, sometimes called the evidence. It asks us to add up the likelihood over every possible value of $\theta$. For a one-dimensional toy problem that may be manageable; for a useful model, it is usually not. Sampling is one of the ways around that obstacle.

A Small Bayesian Update

Before worrying about difficult posteriors, it helps to see what an update feels like. Imagine an unknown coin bias $\theta$. A Beta prior, $\theta \sim \operatorname{Beta}(\alpha, \beta)$, is convenient here: it lets us treat $\alpha$ and $\beta$ roughly like prior heads and prior tails. After observing $h$ heads and $t$ tails, the posterior is simply

\[\theta \mid D \sim \operatorname{Beta}(\alpha + h, \beta + t).\]

The two boxes on the left are your assumptions before data. Try a prior of 8 heads and 2 tails, for example: you start out rather convinced the coin favours heads. Then change the observed heads and tails. The dotted curve is what you started with; the rust curve is where the evidence moves you. This is the basic pattern we want to retain when the update is no longer analytically friendly.

Interactive

Update a coin-bias belief

First choose your prior belief, then add the coin flips you observed. You can drag the sliders or type a number.

Monte Carlo Estimation

Now forget coins for a moment. Suppose we want the area under a function $f(x)$ between $a$ and $b$. The familiar approach is integration. Monte Carlo does something more indirect: sample points $x_i$ uniformly in that interval, look at their heights $f(x_i)$, and average them.

If $X \sim \operatorname{Uniform}(a,b)$, then

\[\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = (b-a)\,\mathbb{E}[f(X)] \approx \frac{b-a}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N f(x_i).\]

There is nothing magical hidden in the approximation. The average height of enough randomly chosen points approaches the average height of the function, and average height times width is area. The law of large numbers does the rest.

Try changing the function and the number of samples. Each dot shows one random place where we looked at the function. The estimate changes with every resample, but it settles down as $N$ grows. That noisy convergence is a useful intuition for most Monte Carlo algorithms.

Interactive

Estimate an area with random points

Change the sample count, then press resample a few times. Watch the estimate become less jumpy as you add more dots.

More generally, if $X \sim p(x)$, then

\[\mathbb{E}_{p}[f(X)] = \int f(x)p(x)\,dx \approx \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N f(x_i).\]

This is the whole promise and the whole catch: the approximation is easy once we have samples from $p$. What if $p$ itself is a complicated posterior?

For easy distributions, inverse-transform sampling gives one answer. Draw $U \sim \operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)$ and set $X = F^{-1}(U)$, where $F$ is the cumulative distribution function. But many useful $F^{-1}$ functions have no neat closed form. That is why we need other ways of turning easy randomness into harder randomness.

Sampling from a Posterior

Returning to Bayes’ rule, the posterior is proportional to the product of a likelihood and a prior:

\[p(\theta \mid D) \propto p(D \mid \theta)p(\theta).\]

Even when we cannot calculate the evidence $p(D)$, we can often calculate the right-hand side. It is useful to call it an unnormalised score:

\[\tilde{p}(\theta \mid D) = p(D \mid \theta)p(\theta).\]

It does not integrate to one, so it is not quite a probability density yet. Still, it tells us which values of $\theta$ look better relative to one another. Many sampling algorithms only need those relative scores, so the troublesome normalising constant never has to be computed explicitly.

Rejection Sampling

Rejection sampling is the most visual example. Start with a proposal distribution $q(\theta)$ that is easy to draw from. Then place an envelope above the unnormalised target, choosing $M$ large enough that

\[\tilde{p}(\theta \mid D) \leq Mq(\theta) \quad \text{for every } \theta.\]

Draw a candidate $\theta \sim q(\theta)$ and a uniform number $u \sim \operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)$. Keep the candidate when

\[u \leq \frac{\tilde{p}(\theta \mid D)}{Mq(\theta)}.\]

Geometrically, we are throwing points into the envelope and keeping the ones under the target curve. The accepted points have the target distribution. The demo uses a uniform proposal for a Beta-shaped target: rust points survive, grey points do not. Adjust the two shape parameters to see why a loose envelope makes the method inefficient.

Interactive

Keep points under a target curve

Change the shape of the target, then draw a new batch. Every point begins equally likely in the rectangle; only the points below the solid curve are kept.

The method is wonderfully direct, but it has an obvious weakness. If the proposal puts little mass where the posterior is large, the envelope must be tall and most candidates will be rejected. Better proposals, importance sampling, and Markov chain Monte Carlo are all different ways of dealing with that same problem.
entry.summary: A friendly route from Bayes' rule to Monte Carlo and rejection sampling.
